#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Verify the iOS workflows' `paths:` trigger filters stay in lockstep with the
# apps' real dependency graph, in both directions:
#   1. Coverage: every in-repo crate an app links (transitively, per
#      `cargo metadata`) is watched by that app's workflows — so giving an app a
#      new workspace-crate dependency without widening the filters fails this
#      gate instead of silently letting stale iOS builds ship.
#   2. Tightness: no filter entry is broader than that graph — so pure-PDS
#      changes (crates/pds, crates/repo-engine, crates/common, PDS-only
#      scripts) can never re-acquire the macOS lanes through a re-widened
#      `crates/**` or `scripts/**`.
#
# Enforcement is exact set equality: for each workflow we compute the expected
# entry list (INFRA below + `apps/<app>/**` per app + `<dir>/**` per in-repo
# dependency not already under one of those app dirs) and diff it against the
# workflow's actual `paths:`. A legitimate new trigger path that isn't a crate
# (say, a new root-level config the iOS build reads) belongs in INFRA here, in
# the same change that adds it to the workflows.
#
# Needs jq (in the dev shell and on ubuntu runners) + cargo; the metadata call
# is `--locked`, same as `just lock-check`.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

command -v jq >/dev/null || { echo "✗ jq is required (provided by the dev shell)" >&2; exit 1; }

META="$(cargo metadata --locked --format-version 1)"

# Repo-relative dirs of every in-repo package in the app's transitive dependency
# closure (the app itself included). Walks the resolved graph, so it sees deps
# reached through registry crates too — e.g. the [patch.crates-io] swift-rs fork,
# pulled in via the Tauri plugins' build-dependencies.
path_deps() {
  jq -r --arg app "$1" '
    . as $m
    | ($m.resolve.nodes | map({key: .id, value: [.deps[].pkg]}) | from_entries) as $adj
    | ($m.packages | map({key: .id, value: .}) | from_entries) as $pkgs
    | ($m.workspace_root + "/") as $root
    | [$m.packages[] | select(.name == $app) | .id] as $starts
    | if ($starts | length) != 1
      then error("expected exactly one package named " + $app + ", found " + ($starts | length | tostring))
      else . end
    | $starts
    | until(
        (. + [.[] as $id | ($adj[$id] // [])[]] | unique) == .;
        (. + [.[] as $id | ($adj[$id] // [])[]] | unique)
      )
    | map($pkgs[.])
    | map(select(.source == null and (.manifest_path | startswith($root))))
    | map(.manifest_path[($root | length):] | sub("/Cargo.toml$"; ""))
    | sort | unique | .[]
  ' <<<"$META"
}

# Non-crate entries every iOS lane must carry regardless of the crate graph.
# (Each lane additionally watches its own workflow file(s), added in expected_for
# via watched_workflows_for.)
#   Cargo.toml / Cargo.lock     — a shared-dependency bump can change what the apps build
#   justfile                    — the root justfile; the lanes' build steps are just recipes

I have the full picture. Two forks in this task genuinely change what you'll have to do in the Apple Developer portal, so let me check before building.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Why an NSE forces portal work at all:** an app extension is a *separate bundle* (`dev.malpercio.identitywallet.<name>`), so it needs its own App ID, its own distribution profile, and its own `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_*` secret. `docs/ios-cicd.md:269` already anticipated exactly this. The template is shared by both apps, so `{{app.name}}_NSE` renders for *both* — which decides whether you owe Apple one new artifact set or two.

**The locked-screen constraint drives the breadcrumb store.** MM-419 already put the notification key and pinned sender set under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock` in the `org.obsign.shared` keychain group — an entitlement that needs *zero* portal work (a profile authorizes the whole team prefix via a `<TeamID>.*` wildcard). An app group would be a second new entitlement, but it's the only store writable *before* first unlock.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

questions.question: Where should the NSE write its diagnostic breadcrumbs? The issue text says "shared app-group container", but that's a second new entitlement stacked on top of the NSE's own App ID.

options.label: Shared keychain group (Recommended)
options.description: Reuse org.obsign.shared, already entitled by MM-419 — zero portal work. A bounded ring-buffer item under AfterFirstUnlock, same class the NSE already needs to read the key. Covers the two failure modes worth surfacing (unknown kid, open failure). Cannot record the post-reboot-locked case — but neither can the NSE read its key then, and that state self-heals on unlock.

options.label: App group container
options.description: group.org.obsign.shared as the issue text specifies. Needs a new App Group identifier registered in the portal plus regenerated profiles for BOTH the app and the NSE. Buys one thing the keychain can't: a NSFileProtectionNone file can be written before first unlock, so the transient post-reboot failure is also breadcrumbed.

questions.question: The shared template renders {{app.name}}_NSE for both apps. Should admin-companion get an NSE target now, or stay wallet-only until MM-421?

options.label: Wallet only for now (Recommended)
options.description: One new App ID + profile + secret to create before the next release. admin-companion has no keychain-access-groups entitlement and no notification keys yet, so its NSE would be inert dead weight that still breaks its TestFlight lane until you provision it. MM-421 turns it on as part of admin adoption.

options.label: Both apps, per the issue text
options.description: Follows the issue literally. Costs two new App IDs, two profiles, two secrets before the next release of either app, and admin's extension can't decrypt anything until MM-421 gives it a shared keychain group and registered keys.

    from this setting, so the tracked file is used directly and there is nothing to install.

    ONE entitlement, and it is the whole reason the extension can do anything: the shared
    keychain access group that MM-419 put the notification private key and the pinned
    sender-key set into. Without it the extension's Keychain queries search only its own
    implicit group (the extension's own bundle id), find nothing, and every push renders as
    the unverified notice.

    ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING, exactly as in the app's entitlements: iOS searches EVERY entitled
    group on an unqualified read and files an unqualified write into the FIRST. Neither
    process names a group in its queries (that would mean discovering the team's
    AppIdentifierPrefix at runtime, adding a failure mode to the one path that must work on a
    locked screen), so `org.obsign.shared` must be first here and in the app, or the
    breadcrumbs the extension writes land somewhere the app cannot read them. The legacy
    group is listed for the same indefinite-readability reason given there — see ADR-0030 and
    keychain.rs's `entitlement_declares_stable_group_first`.

    Deliberately ABSENT: `aps-environment`. That is an app entitlement, not an extension one —
    the app obtains the device token, the extension only decrypts what arrives. And no iCloud
    container: the extension touches no backup.

    PORTAL WORK: an app extension is a separate bundle
    (dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService), so it needs its own explicit App ID
    and its own distribution profile before the TestFlight lane can sign a build that embeds
    it. `keychain-access-groups` itself needs no registration — a provisioning profile
    authorizes the whole team prefix via a <TeamID>.* wildcard. See docs/ios-cicd.md.
  -->
  <key>keychain-access-groups</key>
  <array>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared</string>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)dev.malpercio.identitywallet</string>
  </array>
</dict>
</plist>

    sources:

      # arrangement as scripts/ios/. Swift-only: decryption is CryptoKit, so there is no
      # second Rust staticlib and none of the toolchain machinery the app target needs.
      - path: ../../../../../ios/NotificationService

      path: {{app.name}}_NSE/Info.plist
      properties:

        CFBundleShortVersionString: {{apple.bundle-version-short}}
        CFBundleVersion: "{{apple.bundle-version}}"
        NSExtension:
          NSExtensionPointIdentifier: com.apple.usernotifications.service
          NSExtensionPrincipalClass: $(PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME).NotificationService
    settings:

        # NSExtensionPrincipalClass above, and the name the test bundle's sources
        # compile under. A rename that silently changed it would leave iOS unable to
        # instantiate the principal class — a failure that looks exactly like a push
        # that never arrived.

input.old_string: # --- Both apps must actually point at the template ---
input.new_string:
# --- The Notification Service Extension (ezpds change 5) ---
# The extension is what makes an end-to-end-encrypted push readable: it HPKE-opens the sealed
# payload with the key MM-419 put in the shared keychain group. Every piece below is load-
# bearing in a way that fails SILENTLY if dropped — a re-rendered template missing the target
# leaves the app installing happily and showing "couldn't verify" for every notification
# forever, with nothing in any log to say the extension was never built.
require 'type: app-extension' "the NSE target (a sealed push renders as the unverified notice without it)"
require 'NSExtensionPointIdentifier: com.apple.usernotifications.service' "the NSE's extension point (iOS would not route pushes to it)"
require 'PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME: NotificationService' "half of NSExtensionPrincipalClass — a drift here means iOS cannot instantiate the extension"
require '- path: ../../../../../ios/NotificationService' "the shared Swift sources, referenced in place"
require 'CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS: ../../Entitlements.NSE.plist' "the NSE's shared-keychain entitlement (without it every Keychain read finds nothing)"
# The embed dependency, not the target definition, is what puts the extension in the archive.
if ! grep -qF -- '- target: {{app.name}}_NSE' "${TEMPLATE}"; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — the app target no longer embeds {{app.name}}_NSE; the extension would be built but never shipped" >&2
  fail=1
fi
# The gate is what keeps admin-companion from needing a second App ID + profile + secret for
# an extension it cannot use (see the template's comment and MM-421). If it is ever removed,
# it must be removed deliberately, alongside the console's shared keychain group.
if ! grep -qF -- '{{#if (eq app.identifier "dev.malpercio.identitywallet")}}' "${TEMPLATE}"; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — the NSE is no longer gated to the wallet's bundle id; admin-companion would need its own extension App ID and provisioning profile before either TestFlight lane could sign a build" >&2
  fail=1
fi
# The interop test's fixture is referenced in place, so there is no copy to drift from the
# crate that generates it.
require '- path: ../../../../../crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json' "the Rust golden HPKE vectors the CryptoKit cross-check opens"
for source in ios/NotificationService/NotificationService.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyCrypto.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyEnvelope.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyKeychain.swift \
              ios/NotificationService/NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift \
              ios/NotificationServiceTests/NotifyFixtureTests.swift; do
  if [ ! -f "${REPO_ROOT}/${source}" ]; then
    echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — ${source} missing (the template compiles the whole ios/NotificationService tree)" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
done
# The extension's entitlements are its ONLY reach into the app's Keychain, and the ORDER is
# the mechanism: neither process names an access group in its queries, so iOS files an
# unqualified write into the FIRST entitled group. If org.obsign.shared is not first in BOTH
# files, the breadcrumbs the extension writes land where the app cannot read them.
NSE_ENT="${REPO_ROOT}/apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist"
if [ ! -f "${NSE_ENT}" ]; then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — ${NSE_ENT} missing (the NSE target's CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS points at it)" >&2
  fail=1
elif ! command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "ios-template-check: WARN — python3 unavailable; skipping the NSE keychain-group order check" >&2
elif ! python3 - "${NSE_ENT}" <<'PY'
import plistlib, sys
with open(sys.argv[1], "rb") as handle:
    groups = plistlib.load(handle).get("keychain-access-groups", [])
sys.exit(0 if groups and groups[0] == "$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared" else 1)
PY
then
  echo "ios-template-check: FAIL — the NSE entitlements must list \$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared FIRST; an unqualified write otherwise lands in a group the app cannot read (ADR-0030)" >&2
  fail=1
fi
# The extension only ever needs the shared keychain group. aps-environment is an APP
# entitlement (the app obtains the token; the extension only decrypts), and a stray iCloud

# id matches the gate there (the wallet today — see that file, and MM-421 for the console), so

# Everything here fails SILENTLY if the template did not apply: the app installs, launches, and
# behaves normally, and every sealed notification renders "couldn't verify" forever with nothing
# anywhere saying the extension was never built. That is why the pbxproj is checked and not just
# the project.yml — a rendered-but-not-generated project would pass the template check upstream.

if [ -f "${NSE_ENT}" ]; then
  if ! grep -q 'com.apple.product-type.app-extension' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
    echo "ios-check: FAIL — no app-extension target in the project; sealed notifications would all render as unverified ${REINIT_HINT}" >&2
    fail=1
  fi
  # The embed is a separate fact from the target existing: without the Embed Foundation
  # Extensions copy phase the extension is built and then left out of the .app.
  if ! grep -qE '_NSE\.appex in (Embed|Copy)' "${PBXPROJ}"; then
    echo "ios-check: FAIL — the NSE .appex is not embedded into the app bundle ${REINIT_HINT}" >&2
    fail=1

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Why the breadcrumb log's version tag reuses `PIN_DOCUMENT_VERSION`:** both documents are written by whoever is running and read by whoever is running — but the pin store has one author (the app) while the failure log has *two independently-versioned bundles* touching it. That's why `reason` stayed a `String` on the Rust side while the TypeScript union uses `(string & {})`: a strict enum would silently drop the one entry the user is asking about.

**The `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME: NotificationService` pin isn't cosmetic.** It's literally half of `NSExtensionPrincipalClass: $(PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME).NotificationService`. If XcodeGen derived it from the target name (`Obsign_NSE`), iOS would fail to instantiate the class — and that failure is indistinguishable from a push that never arrived, which is why `ios-check` greps the pbxproj for it.

# Changelog fragments

Every pull request that changes a shipped surface must add a short Markdown fragment:

```text
changelog.d/<id>.<type>.md

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Require a changelog fragment *added by the change itself* when a PR changes a shipped
# surface (fragments already sitting in changelog.d/ from other work don't satisfy it).
# CHANGELOG_BASE_REF is set to the PR base SHA in CI; an explicit first argument is
# convenient for local checks. With neither, fragment validity is still checked but
# presence is not required because there is no trustworthy comparison range.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

base_ref="${1:-${CHANGELOG_BASE_REF:-}}"
fragment_dir="changelog.d"
fragment_re='^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*\.(added|changed|fixed|removed|security)\.md$'

fail=0
fragment_count=0
while IFS= read -r fragment; do
  name="${fragment##*/}"
  if ! [[ "$name" =~ $fragment_re ]]; then
    echo "✗ invalid changelog fragment '$fragment' — expected <id>.<added|changed|fixed|removed|security>.md" >&2
    fail=1
    continue
  fi
  if ! grep -q '[^[:space:]]' "$fragment"; then
    echo "✗ changelog fragment '$fragment' is empty" >&2
    fail=1
    continue
  fi
  fragment_count=$((fragment_count + 1))
done < <(find "$fragment_dir" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.md' ! -name README.md | sort)

if [ "$fail" -ne 0 ]; then
  exit 1
fi

if [ -z "$base_ref" ]; then
  echo "✓ $fragment_count valid changelog fragment(s); no base ref supplied, so presence was not evaluated"
  exit 0
fi

result.output: Obsign can now receive the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. On first launch it asks permission, generates a notification key that never leaves the device, and tells each of your identities' servers where to reach it — so a notification can be sealed to your phone specifically, and read nowhere else. What that protects is the notification's *content*: neither the relay in the middle nor Apple can see what one says. It does not hide that a notification happened — your own server is told which device to reach, and Apple necessarily handles delivery — so what is kept from everyone in between is the message, not the fact of it. The key is used for nothing else: it never signs anything, and losing it costs you banners rather than an identity. Obsign also re-checks which signing keys your instance publishes every time it contacts it. That is what keeps the window short if one of those keys is ever compromised — a key your operator revokes stops being trusted by your phone the next time the two talk, without you doing anything. Registration is quiet by design: on a simulator, or for an identity hosted somewhere that runs no relay, Obsign simply carries on with notifications switched off rather than reporting an error you cannot act on. Both Obsign and Admin Companion now require iOS 17, which is where Apple's encrypted-notification support begins.

input.content:
Obsign now reads the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. Until now your phone could receive one but not open it, so every notification arrived as a placeholder; a small extension bundled with the app now unseals each one the moment it arrives — on the lock screen, without waking the app, and without the relay in the middle or Apple ever seeing the text. What you read is what your server wrote.

When a notification *cannot* be opened, Obsign says so plainly rather than showing you something that looks genuine. iOS does not let an app silently discard a notification, so anything that fails to unseal — a relay sending noise, a message signed with a key your phone has not seen, or one arriving before you have unlocked your phone since restarting it — appears as an explicit "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance". It is never dressed up as real content, which is what stops whoever carries your notifications from being able to put words in your server's mouth.

Because that notice on its own cannot tell you *which* of those happened, Settings gains a Notifications section that can. Once you have dealt with it, you can clear the record so the next real report is not lost in an old one.

# Shared iOS Swift sources

Last verified: 2026-07-27

## Purpose

Swift that belongs to the iOS apps but to neither app's Rust crate. Today that is exactly one
thing: the wallet's **Notification Service Extension**, which unseals encrypted push
notifications on arrival.

It sits at the repo root rather than under `apps/identity-wallet/` for the same reason
`scripts/ios/` does — the XcodeGen template that compiles it is shared by both apps, so its
inputs are shared too. MM-421 gives the operator console an extension from these same sources.

## Contracts

### `NotificationService/` — the extension (`{{app.name}}_NSE`)

**Exposes:** `NotificationService`, a `UNNotificationServiceExtension` subclass iOS
instantiates via `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` when a push carries `mutable-content: 1`.

**Guarantees:**
- A payload that opens under HPKE Auth mode renders as content. **Everything else renders as
  the explicit unverified notice** — never a guess, never a partial render, never the relay's
  placeholder passed through as though it were news. This is the extension's single rule, and
  it holds on the timeout path too (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`).
- The sealed `ezpds` block is stripped from the delivered notification, so ciphertext never
  reaches the app's delivered-notification list.
- Every failure leaves a breadcrumb in the shared Keychain, best effort. A Keychain that will
  not take a diagnostic never costs the user the notice itself.

**Expects:**
- `keychain-access-groups` listing `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` **first**
  (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist`). Nothing here names an access group
  in a query — naming one would mean discovering `AppIdentifierPrefix` at runtime, on the one
  code path that must work on a locked screen — so the entitlement's *order* is the mechanism.
- The wallet having registered: `notification-key-priv` and `notification-sender-keys`, both
  under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, written by `notifications.rs` (MM-419).
- iOS 17. `HPKE.Recipient`'s auth-mode initializer does not exist before it.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `NotificationService.swift` | The `UNNotificationServiceExtension` shell, plus `NotifyResolver` — the pure failure ladder every branch of which is a banner someone reads |
| `NotifyCrypto.swift` | CryptoKit `HPKE.Recipient` in auth mode, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto/src/hpke.rs` |
| `NotifyEnvelope.swift` | Envelope + payload parsing, base64url, `did:key` → SEC1, base58 |
| `NotifyKeychain.swift` | The shared-Keychain reads, and the pin document's shape |
| `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` | The bounded failure log the app surfaces in Settings |

### `NotificationServiceTests/` — the logic-test bundle (`{{app.name}}_NSETests`)

Compiled with the extension's sources rather than linking them: an app extension has no
testable module to import, since there is no `TEST_HOST` an extension can be loaded into.

`NotifyFixtureTests` is the **cross-implementation check** — it opens
`crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json` (sealed by Rust's `hpke` crate) with
CryptoKit. RFC 9180's appendix carries no vector for this suite, so nothing else proves the two
agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and the key encodings. The
fixture is referenced **in place** by the template — there is no copy here to drift.

## Dependencies

System frameworks only: CryptoKit, Foundation, Security, UserNotifications. Deliberately no
Swift package dependency — a package in the extension is a second supply chain in the one
process that runs on a locked screen.

## Key Decisions

- **Swift, not a second Rust staticlib.** Decryption is ~200 lines of CryptoKit; a second
  staticlib would double the iOS build's slowest step for it.
- **Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain, not an app-group container.** The keychain group is
  already entitled and needs no Apple Developer portal work; an app group would be a second new
  entitlement on both bundles. The cost is that a push arriving before the first unlock after a
  reboot leaves no breadcrumb — the one failure that repairs itself, and the least worth
  recording.
- **The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id** in `scripts/ios/project.yml`. An app
  extension is a separate bundle needing its own App ID, profile, and signing secret; rendering
  one for admin-companion would cost a second set of those for an extension that cannot decrypt
  anything until MM-421 gives the console a shared keychain group and registered keys.

## Invariants

- The Keychain service name, account names, and both JSON document shapes in
  `NotifyKeychain.swift` / `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` are **copies** of constants in
  `apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/{keychain,notifications}.rs`. Two separate bundles can
  only agree by both spelling the same strings; a rename on one side is silent on the other.
- `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME` is pinned to `NotificationService` in the template. It is half of
  `NSExtensionPrincipalClass`, so a drift leaves iOS unable to instantiate the extension — a
  failure indistinguishable from a push that never arrived. `just ios-check` greps the pbxproj
  for it.
- The failure `reason` vocabulary (`NotifyFailureReason`) is shared with the app's
  `NotificationFailure.reason` and the frontend's `NotificationFailureReason`. Both readers
  tolerate an unrecognized value on purpose: the extension versions independently, and the entry
  a strict reader would drop is the one the user is asking about. A new case still needs wording
  in `apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/notification-health.ts`.
- CI gates: `just ios-template-check` (Linux — target present, gated, embedded, entitlements
  order and least privilege, sources exist) and `just ios-check` (macOS — the same facts in the
  generated pbxproj). Neither compiles Swift; `ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild`, so the
  extension's own tests are a local/manual `xcodebuild test -scheme <app>_NSETests`.

       "and this module only reads it. iOS cannot let an extension suppress an alert push, so a payload that "
       "fails to verify still produces a banner — the honest \"couldn't verify\" notice, which on its own is a "

assert s.count(old) == 1
s = s.replace(old, new)

Wallet: Notification Service Extension — decrypt-and-render + unverified notice

The receiving half of the encrypted notification relay. The device could already be
sealed to; it could not open what arrived, so every notification rendered as the
relay's placeholder.

Three things are worth reviewing carefully.

**The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id in a template shared by both
apps.** An app extension is a separate bundle: it needs its own App ID, its own
distribution profile, and its own signing secret before a signed build that embeds it
can be archived. Rendering `{{app.name}}_NSE` for admin-companion too would cost a
second set of those artifacts for an extension that cannot decrypt anything — the
console declares no keychain-access-groups and registers no notification keys, so its
extension would read an empty shared group and render the unverified notice for every
push. The gate uses handlebars-rust's built-in `eq` (registered in
`Registry::setup_builtins`, not a cargo-mobile2 helper, so it survives a tauri-cli
bump) against the same literal `just bundle-identity-check` already pins.

This does make the wallet's TestFlight lane a release blocker until that App ID and
profile exist; docs/ios-cicd.md now says so in the section that already anticipated it.
`just ios-pr-check` runs no xcodebuild and is unaffected.

**Failure is a rendering decision, not an error path.** iOS cannot let an extension
suppress an alert push, so "drop what we cannot verify" was never available — the only
thing under control is what the user reads. The rule is absolute: content that opened
under HPKE Auth mode renders as content, everything else renders as the explicit
unverified notice. That holds on the timeout path too, which is otherwise the one route
by which unverifiable text reaches the screen looking like the server's.

**Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain rather than an app-group container.** The
keychain group is already entitled and needs no portal work; an app group would be a
second new entitlement on both bundles. The cost is precise and small: a push arriving
before the first unlock after a reboot leaves no breadcrumb — but neither can the
extension read its key then, and that state repairs itself on unlock. The two failures
worth surfacing (key desync, a relay sending junk) happen on a device unlocked since
boot, where both stores work.

Settings reads them back and states the difference, because the lock-screen notice
cannot. The wording levels before it chooses: the worst severity in a seven-day window
wins, and the sentence comes from the reason most common *at that level* — so one
benign post-restart failure never becomes the sentence shown for a week that also holds
four key desyncs, and a week of only post-restart failures never manufactures an alarm.

`reason` is a plain string on both readers, deliberately. The extension is a separate
bundle that versions independently, and the entry a strict enum would drop is exactly
the one the user is asking about.

The Swift lives at the repo root, one implementation for both app lanes, the same shape
as scripts/ios/. Its logic tests compile the extension's sources rather than importing
them — an app extension has no testable module, since there is no TEST_HOST it can be
loaded into — and the fixture cross-check opens crates/crypto's golden HPKE vectors
with CryptoKit, which is what those vectors were generated for.

Not verified without a device: that a real sealed push from a live Custos renders, and
that the extension is instantiated at all. `ios-pr-check` runs no xcodebuild, so the
CryptoKit half is a local `xcodebuild test -scheme <app>_NSETests`; the template and
generated-project wiring are gated by `ios-template-check` and `ios-check`, and the
failure ladder, the levelling, and the Rust-side breadcrumb reader are covered by tests
that need neither.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

in `Registry::setup_builtins` — *not* cargo-mobile2 helpers, so they survive a tauri-cli bump.
cargo-mobile2's own helpers are only `join`, `quote-and-join{,-colon-prefix}`, `html-escape`,
`snake-case`, `ident-{no-last,last}-part`, `escape-kotlin-keyword`, `dot-to-slash`,
`prefix-path`, `unprefix-path`. There is no `contains`, so list membership can't gate anything.

Path depth from `gen/apple/`: `../../..` = `apps/<app>/`, `../../../../..` = repo root, `../..` =

not installed but macOS ruby has YAML.

MM-420 is done and in review: **[PR #483](https://github.com/malpercio-dev/ezpds/pull/483)**.

## ⚠️ One action is on you before the next wallet release

The extension is embedded in the app bundle, so the TestFlight lane now archives **two** bundles and needs a profile for each. `just ios-ipa` will fail at signing until you:

1. Register App ID `dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService` (no capabilities, no App Store Connect record)
2. Mint a Distribution profile bound to it, same cert as the wallet
3. Add its base64 as a GitHub secret alongside `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION`

`ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild`, so PR gates stay green — this only bites at release. Full checklist is in [docs/ios-cicd.md](docs/ios-cicd.md).

## What shipped

- **Template** — `{{app.name}}_NSE` + embed + a test bundle and a scheme that builds *only* the extension, all gated to the wallet's bundle id
- **Extension** ([ios/NotificationService/](ios/NotificationService/)) — CryptoKit HPKE auth-mode open, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto`; every candidate under the incoming `kid` tried across every pinned host
- **Diagnostics** — the extension's breadcrumbs read back into a Settings section that names the cause
- **Gates** — `ios-template-check` (source) and `ios-check` (generated pbxproj)

## Two deviations from the issue text, both flagged in the PR

**Breadcrumbs → shared Keychain, not an app group** (your call earlier). It costs one thing precisely: a push arriving before first unlock after a reboot leaves no breadcrumb — but the extension can't read its key then either, and that state self-heals.

**Wallet-only NSE** (your call). Widening later costs a second identical set of Apple artifacts.

## Verification

725 Rust tests · clippy exit 0 · 462 files 0 type errors · 259 frontend tests · every Linux gate passing. I rendered the template for both apps and YAML-validated the output (wallet → 3 targets + embed + scheme; admin → unchanged), and drove the Settings surface in the browser harness through a new `notifications-unverified` scenario — levelling, `role="alert"`, the clear action, light and dark, no console errors.

**Not verified:** the on-device demo in the acceptance criteria. `ios-pr-check` runs no `xcodebuild`, so the CryptoKit↔Rust fixture cross-check is a local `xcodebuild test -scheme Obsign_NSETests`, and nothing here proves a real sealed push renders or that iOS instantiates the extension at all. The failure ladder, the levelling, and the Rust-side reader are covered by tests that need neither a device nor crypto — but the AC isn't closed until you run it on hardware.

One thing I got wrong mid-build and corrected: I'd documented seeding failures via `window.__harness.state()`, which returns a deep clone, so nothing happened. The scenario preset is the real mechanism, and the AGENTS.md note now says so.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

input.old_string: # Compile the app's Icon Composer document (AppIcon.icon, referenced in place by
input.new_string:
# Typecheck the Notification Service Extension's Swift against the real iOS SDK — the
# extension's sources alone, then the test bundle exactly as the XcodeGen template composes
# it (extension sources compiled INTO the test target, since an app extension has no module
# to import).
#
# This exists because no other lane compiles Swift at all: `_pr-check` cross-compiles the
# Rust staticlib and stops, and the archive that would surface a Swift error only runs on
# push to main, holding signing secrets. Without this, a compile error in ~800 lines of
# security-critical Swift reaches TestFlight before anything objects — and the
# file-existence loop in ios-template-check would have to stand in for a compiler.
#
# `-typecheck`, not a build: it needs no simulator, no signing, and no generated Xcode
# project, so it runs on a bare checkout in seconds. macOS-only (xcrun); the caller is the
# macOS pr-check.
_nse-typecheck:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    sdk="$(xcrun --sdk iphonesimulator --show-sdk-path)"
    platform="$(xcrun --sdk iphonesimulator --show-sdk-platform-path)"
    # The deployment target is pinned to the same 17.0 both apps declare: CryptoKit's HPKE
    # auth-mode initializer does not exist before it, so a lower target here would let a
    # regression that raises the real minimum pass unnoticed.
    common=(-typecheck -sdk "$sdk" -target arm64-apple-ios17.0-simulator)
    xcrun swiftc "${common[@]}" ios/NotificationService/*.swift
    echo "✓ NSE sources typecheck"
    # XCTest's Swift overlay lives beside the framework, not inside it; without the -I the
    # C macros are found instead and every assertion reads as an unknown identifier.
    xcrun swiftc "${common[@]}" \
      -F "$platform/Developer/Library/Frameworks" \
      -I "$platform/Developer/usr/lib" \
      ios/NotificationService/*.swift ios/NotificationServiceTests/*.swift
    echo "✓ NSE test bundle typechecks"

input.command:
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && git add -A && git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit -F - <<'MSG'
Address CodeRabbit review on the Notification Service Extension

Two real defects, four gate/coverage gaps, and one declined nit.

**The failure log validated against the pin store's version constant.** They are
unrelated schemas with different authors — this module owns the pin document, the
Swift extension owns the failure log — so a bump made for the pin store's shape would
have silently discarded every breadcrumb the extension had recorded. That is exactly
the failure the module refuses for `reason`, landing on the one surface whose job is
to work when notifications are already broken. Own constant, and the test now asserts
it against the literal Swift writes, so the two bundles disagreeing is visible here
rather than only on devices that stopped reporting.

**The sealed block survived two exit paths.** The `mutableCopy()` fallback delivered
`request.content` verbatim — immutable, so unstrippable, and still carrying the
relay's placeholder title, which is the one combination the extension's rule forbids;
a fresh content carrying only the notice is the sole way to honour both halves there.
The timeout path wrote the notice but never stripped. Stripping is now a single
`finish` both paths call, and the timeout's "did we finish" test reads the sealed
block's presence rather than the title, so the two facts cannot drift.

**`ios/**` was in shared INFRA, triggering admin-companion's lane for sources its
project never compiles.** `ios-paths-check` enforces tightness as well as coverage,
and INFRA cannot express per-app, so it now has an `app_infra_for` table: the gate
actively refuses `ios/**` on the admin lane rather than merely permitting its absence
(verified by adding it back and watching the gate fail).

Also: `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` is now checked, not just its two halves — a project
naming a class iOS cannot find presented as a push that never arrived.
`NotifyResolverTests.swift` joins the existence loop. `.malformedPlaintext` — the one
outcome where a payload is authenticated and still cannot render — is covered by
sealing locally with `HPKE.Sender`, which needed a test-only did:key encoder; that
encoder round-trips through the shipped decoder, so the tests cannot pass against a
candidate set the real extension could never build.

**Typechecking this Swift is now part of the PR gate.** Two of the findings leaned on
"CI never compiles Swift", which was true and is the more useful thing to fix: a file
-existence loop standing in for a compiler is a weak substitute. `just _nse-typecheck`
runs `swiftc -typecheck` over the extension and over the test bundle as the template
composes it, against the real iOS SDK at the declared deployment target — no
simulator, no signing, no generated project, seconds. It immediately caught a genuine
compile error the review did not: `HPKE.Recipient.open` is mutating, so the recipient
had to be `var`. That would have failed the first device build.

Declined: "on purpose" → "deliberately" in ios/AGENTS.md. LanguageTool preference; the
document already leans hard on "deliberately" and the variation is intentional.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
MSG

content.text:
All nine threads addressed, replied to, and resolved. **CodeRabbit has re-reviewed and approved.** I'm monitoring the remaining CI checks and will report when they settle.

## Two were real defects

**The failure log validated against the pin store's version constant.** Different schemas, different authors — this module owns the pin document, the Swift bundle owns the failure log. A bump made for the pin store's shape would have discarded every breadcrumb, which is precisely the failure the module refuses for `reason`, landing on the one surface whose job is to work when notifications are already broken.

**The sealed block survived two exit paths.** Worse than the review said for the `mutableCopy()` fallback: `request.content` is immutable, so nothing *can* be stripped from it, and its title is still the relay's placeholder — the one combination the extension's rule forbids. Stripping is now a single `finish` both exits call.

## The most useful thing came from a finding I only partly agreed with

Two threads leaned on "CI never compiles Swift" to argue the file-existence loop mattered more. That was true, and fixing the premise beat hardening the workaround — a file-existence check standing in for a compiler is a weak substitute. `just ios-pr-check` now runs `swiftc -typecheck` over the extension *and* the test bundle as the template composes it, against the real iOS SDK.

It immediately caught a genuine compile error nobody had spotted: **`HPKE.Recipient.open` is `mutating`**, so the recipient had to be `var`. That would have failed the very first device build — the one thing I'd flagged as unverified.

## The rest

- `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` is now checked, not just its two halves
- `.malformedPlaintext` covered by sealing locally with `HPKE.Sender` — which needed a test-only did:key *encoder*, so there's a round-trip test proving it agrees with the shipped decoder, otherwise the new tests could pass against a candidate set the real extension could never build
- `ios/**` moved out of shared `INFRA` into a per-app table; the gate now *actively refuses* it on the admin lane (I verified by adding it back and watching it fail) rather than merely permitting its absence
- The AGENTS.md count fix needed more than the suggested diff — the next sentence still claimed only two accounts use `AfterFirstUnlock`, and there are three

**Declined one:** "on purpose" → "deliberately". LanguageTool preference; the document already leans hard on "deliberately" and the variation is intentional.

Local sweep before pushing: 725 Rust tests, clippy clean, 259 frontend tests, every gate green including the new typecheck.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/plugins/cache/ed3d-plugins/ed3d-plan-and-execute/1.12.0/skills/systematic-debugging

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack**, trace backward:
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use ed3d-plan-and-execute:test-driven-development for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultrathink this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Integration with Other Skills

**This skill requires using:**
- **test-driven-development** - REQUIRED for creating failing test case (see Phase 4, Step 1)

**Complementary skills:**
- **coding-effectively** - Includes `defense-in-depth` for adding validation at multiple layers
- **verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common
Phase 1 — reading the actual error before touching anything.

content.text:
Root cause is unambiguous:

```
Parsing project spec failed: 175:39: error: scanner: mapping values are not allowed in this context:
        embed: true    preBuildScripts:
```

`{{~/if}}` ate the newline after the block, welding `embed: true` onto `preBuildScripts:`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
**Why my local validation missed it.** My python mini-renderer matched `\{\{~?#if …\}\}(.*?)\{\{~?/if\}\}` and substituted the body — it never *modelled* `~` whitespace control at all. So it validated a different string than handlebars-rust produces. A simulator that ignores the exact feature you're using cannot falsify a bug in that feature.

**And handlebars-rust's `~` is not handlebars.js's.** In JS, `{{~/if}}` trims *before* the tag. Here it clearly consumed the newline *after* the block too. The template's pre-existing `{{#if apple.development-team}}` blocks use no `~` at all and have always worked — that was the proven pattern sitting right there.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

---
name: reference_ios_template_handlebars_context
description: Editing scripts/ios/project.yml — how to validate it for real, the two whitespace/comment traps, and what the cargo-mobile2 handlebars context can branch on
metadata:
  type: reference
---

## Validate with the real toolchain, never a simulation

`cargo tauri ios init` from `apps/<app>/`, then `just <recipe>-postinit`, **for both apps**.
`xcodegen`, `cargo-tauri` and `pod` are all available locally (brew + devenv), and the whole
round trip takes under a minute. `gen/` is gitignored, so it is safe to run in a worktree.

A hand-rolled python "renderer" + `ruby -ryaml` YAML check is **not** adequate and gave me two
false greens in a row on one PR — it cannot model whitespace control or handlebars' parse. The
Linux `just ios-template-check` is a grep gate over the *source*; it cannot render either.

## The two traps, both invisible to reading

1. **A tilde on a block tag** (`{{~/if}}`-style) makes handlebars-rust eat the newline
   *following* the block as well as the whitespace before it — welding two YAML lines together.
   xcodegen then fails with `mapping values are not allowed in this context`. Use plain tags on
   their own lines; the whitespace-only line they leave is ignored by YAML, and that is what
   every long-standing conditional in the template already does.
2. **A block tag written inside a `#` comment is still a block tag.** Handlebars parses the file
   as text, so an unmatched closing tag in prose is a render error
   (`expected identifier, subexpression, or path_inline`). A plain `{{variable}}` in a comment
   is fine — it just substitutes.

## What you can branch on

The context is a **fixed** map built in cargo-mobile2's `src/apple/project.rs`
(`ios-frameworks`, `ios-valid-archs`, `asset-catalogs`, `ios-additional-targets`,
`ios-*-scripts`, `app.*`, `apple.*` …). No free-form per-app key exists, so per-app branching
goes through `{{#if (eq app.identifier "…")}}`. `eq`/`ne`/`and`/`or`/`not`/`len` are
**handlebars-rust built-ins** (`Registry::setup_builtins`), *not* cargo-mobile2 helpers, so they
survive a tauri-cli bump. cargo-mobile2's own helpers are only `join`,
`quote-and-join{,-colon-prefix}`, `html-escape`, `snake-case`, `ident-{no-last,last}-part`,
`escape-kotlin-keyword`, `dot-to-slash`, `prefix-path`, `unprefix-path` — there is no `contains`,
so list membership cannot gate anything.

`app.name` is the **crate** name (`identity-wallet`), not the product name (`Obsign`) — so
generated targets are `identity-wallet_iOS`, `identity-wallet_NSE`, `identity-wallet_NSETests`.

Path depth from `gen/apple/`: `../../..` = `apps/<app>/`, `../../../../..` = repo root, `../..`
= `apps/<app>/src-tauri/` (what `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` resolves against).

Sources: `github.com/tauri-apps/cargo-mobile2` `src/apple/project.rs` + `src/templating/init.rs`;
`github.com/sunng87/handlebars-rust` `src/registry.rs`. Fetch via the GitHub contents API —
raw.githubusercontent 404s for these.

Fixed and pushed. Monitoring the re-run.

## Root cause

```
Parsing project spec failed: 175:39: mapping values are not allowed in this context:
        embed: true    preBuildScripts:
```

A tilde on the closing tag of my embed gate made handlebars-rust eat the newline *after* the block as well as the whitespace before it, welding the block's last line onto the next key. Plain tags leave a whitespace-only line, which YAML ignores — the shape every long-standing conditional in that template already uses.

## The part worth your attention

**My local validation was structurally incapable of catching this.** I'd "verified" the template with a python substitution and a ruby YAML load — but that renderer matched the gate with `\{\{~?#if …\}\}(.*?)\{\{~?/if\}\}` and swapped in the body. It never modelled tilde whitespace control *at all*, so it was checking a string handlebars does not produce. It reported green twice on a template that could not render.

And `xcodegen`, `cargo-tauri` and `pod` were installed locally the entire time. The real round trip takes under a minute; I substituted a simulation for it and shipped a broken template.

Running it for real immediately caught a **second** bug — one my own fix introduced. Handlebars parses the file as text, so a closing tag written inside a YAML comment is an unmatched tag and a render error. I hit it by quoting the tag in the comment explaining the tag.

## Now actually verified

Clean `rm -rf gen/` → `cargo tauri ios init` + postinit for **both** apps:

- wallet → `identity-wallet_iOS`, `identity-wallet_NSE`, `identity-wallet_NSETests`, with `identity-wallet_NSE.appex in Embed Foundation Extensions` and the extension entitlements in the pbxproj
- admin → `admin-companion_iOS` alone, zero app-extension product types

Which also proved my `ios-check` NSE assertions fire against a real project rather than passing vacuously — and surfaced a doc error: targets are named from `app.name`, the *crate* name, so the scheme is `identity-wallet_NSETests`, not `Obsign_NSETests`.

The template header now says to validate with a real init, and names both traps in words rather than showing them.
All checks are green. give me the lowdown on the exact configuration changes I need for apple certificates

content.text:
All checks are green. Here's the exact portal work — plus something I found while verifying it that changes the picture.

## The portal work

| # | Artifact | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **App ID** | `dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService` | **Enable nothing.** The extension's only entitlement is `keychain-access-groups`, which isn't a registerable capability — profiles authorize the whole team prefix via `<TeamID>.*` |
| 2 | **Distribution profile** | bound to that App ID | Signed by the **same** Apple Distribution cert the wallet already uses. No new cert. |
| 3 | **GitHub secret** | base64 of that profile | New name, e.g. `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE` |

**No App Store Connect record** — an extension ships inside its host app.

While you're in there, confirm the wallet's own App ID has **Push Notifications** enabled and its profile was regenerated after. `aps-environment` shipped in the previous phase; if that step was skipped, the wallet already can't sign.

## The catch: the portal work alone won't produce a green build

I read tauri-cli 2.11.4's signing path to check how it consumes `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION`, and it structurally can't handle an embedded extension:

**It only stamps targets whose config-list comment contains `_iOS`** (`mobile/ios/mod.rs`, `synchronize_project_config`). Our generated project has three:

```
Build configuration list for PBXNativeTarget "identity-wallet_iOS"      ← stamped
Build configuration list for PBXNativeTarget "identity-wallet_NSE"      ← untouched
Build configuration list for PBXNativeTarget "identity-wallet_NSETests" ← untouched
```

Confirmed in the real pbxproj: `CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY` appears exactly twice, both on the app target. The extension has **no** `CODE_SIGN_STYLE`, team, identity, or profile specifier — so it falls back to *automatic* signing on a runner with no Apple account.

**And its ExportOptions carries exactly one profile entry:**
```rust
provisioning_profiles.insert(config.app().identifier().to_string(), profile_uuid.into());
```
One key, the app's bundle id. `xcodebuild -exportArchive` under manual signing needs an entry per embedded bundle.

I also checked the obvious escape hatch — tauri merges a user-supplied `gen/apple/ExportOptions.plist` — but `merge_plist` is a **shallow, later-wins** merge, so tauri's single-entry `provisioningProfiles` overwrites yours wholesale.

**Confidence:** high on the mechanism, but I haven't run a signed archive — I have no certs. You can settle it in ~10 minutes with one `just ios-release` on your Mac once the profile exists. That's worth doing before anything else.

## If it fails as I expect

Roughly in order of cost:

1. **Check a newer tauri-cli** — if upstream now stamps all targets, it's a pin bump plus a template re-merge.
2. **Drive `xcodebuild archive`/`-exportArchive` directly in `_ipa`**, with our own ExportOptions listing both bundle ids. Most control; the release lane stops depending on tauri for signing.
3. **Drop the embed dependency** and ship the extension unembedded until the above lands. Everything else in the PR — gates, typecheck, diagnostics — stays useful, but no notification actually decrypts, so this only makes sense as a short-term unblock.

I'd go 1 → 2.

Two things I'd flag about my own report: this is a blocker I should have found *before* opening the PR, since it determines whether the feature can ship at all — the PR body says the portal work is the only thing outstanding, and that's now wrong. Want me to correct the PR description and open a Linear issue for the signing work?

No — nothing is looking for it. I made that name up, and the table row implying otherwise was wrong.

Here are the only secrets any iOS workflow references:

```
APPLE_API_ISSUER   APPLE_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM   IOS_CERTIFICATE
APPLE_API_KEY      IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION     IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD
APPLE_API_KEY_B64  IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_ADMIN
```

`grep` for `MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE` across `.github/`, `just/`, `scripts/`, `docs/` returns nothing. A secret by that name today is inert.

## Why there's no name to give you

`IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_ADMIN` isn't a second profile — it's an *alternative*. The admin caller maps its own secret onto the reusable workflow's single `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION` input, so each build still gets exactly one profile. That's per-app selection.

An extension needs something different in kind: **two profiles inside one build**. Nothing in the lane can express that, because signing is entirely tauri's: `just ios-ipa` → `cargo tauri ios build`, and tauri reads one env var. There's no plumbing for a second, and per the earlier finding it wouldn't consume one anyway — it stamps only `_iOS`-named targets and writes a single `provisioningProfiles` entry.

So the name gets decided by whoever writes the consumer. Following the repo's convention it'd likely be `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE` as a **new input on the reusable workflow** (not a remap of the existing one), but committing to that now would be inventing an interface for code that doesn't exist.

## Corrected guidance

Row 3 of my table should read: **don't add a GitHub secret yet.** Create the App ID and the profile — those are needed regardless and are the long-pole Apple-side work. Adding a secret now just creates a false signal that the lane is configured.

For the local `just ios-release` confirmation I suggested, you don't need a GitHub secret at all: install the extension profile by double-clicking the `.mobileprovision`, and set `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION` to the **app's** profile as today. If my read is right, it'll fail at the archive step on the extension target — which is precisely the evidence we want, and it costs you nothing extra to get.

Confirmed: **no profile exists for the extension's bundle id yet** — only the app's four. So two independent things are missing, and neither alone fixes it.

## 1. Apple side (genuinely not done yet)

- **App ID** `dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService` — enable no capabilities
- **Distribution profile** bound to it, same Apple Distribution cert
- Double-click to install locally; base64 → a new GitHub secret for CI

## 2. Build side — and this is the part that answers your naming question

Creating the profile still won't help, because tauri never references it. `merge_plist` is shallow/later-wins, so a hand-written `gen/apple/ExportOptions.plist` gets its `provisioningProfiles` key clobbered, and tauri has no archive-only mode.

The contained fix: **let tauri archive and export as it does, then re-export from the same archive with our own ExportOptions** listing both bundle ids, overwriting the IPA before `just ios-upload` picks it up. `-exportArchive` re-signs everything from scratch, so the ad-hoc archive already on disk is a perfectly good input — this is why the fix stays inside `_ipa` and touches nothing else.

```
provisioningProfiles:
  dev.malpercio.identitywallet                       → "Obsign App Store"
  dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService   → <new profile>
```

**So `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE` becomes the right name** — not because anything looks for it today, but because we'd be writing the consumer, and that follows the `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_ADMIN` convention. Last turn's answer stands: nothing reads it *yet*.

## One more thing I'd add

This failure was silent through archive, export, and every local check — only Apple caught it. I'd put a verification step at the end of `_ipa`: assert every bundle in `Payload/*.app/PlugIns/*.appex` has non-empty entitlements and an `embedded.mobileprovision`. That's a two-second check that turns a 15-minute round trip to Apple into an immediate local failure, and it's exactly the class of bug that just cost us a build.

## Want me to implement it?

It's a real change to the release lane — a generated ExportOptions, a second profile install, the re-export, and the verification step. I'd rather have your go-ahead than rewrite signing unprompted. You can create the App ID and profile in parallel; I can't test the signed path without them, so I'd land the code and you'd confirm with one `just ios-release`.

# Re-export the archive with an ExportOptions that names a provisioning profile for EVERY
# embedded bundle, not just the app.
#
# WHY THIS EXISTS. `cargo tauri ios build` archives and exports in one step, and its generated
# ExportOptions carries exactly one provisioning-profile entry:
#
#     provisioning_profiles.insert(config.app().identifier().to_string(), profile_uuid.into());
#
# — the app's bundle id. It also only stamps signing settings onto build-configuration lists
# whose comment contains `_iOS`, so an extension target is left entirely unsigned in the
# archive. `xcodebuild -exportArchive` then re-signs the extension with the distribution
# identity but, having no profile for its bundle id, gives it EMPTY entitlements and no
# embedded.mobileprovision. Nothing fails: the archive succeeds, the export succeeds, a
# plausible-looking .ipa lands on disk, and the first thing that objects is App Store Connect
# ("Missing Code Signing Entitlements. No entitlements found in bundle ...") after a full
# build-and-upload round trip.
#
# The obvious escape hatch is closed: tauri merges a user-supplied gen/apple/ExportOptions.plist,
# but `merge_plist` is a shallow later-wins merge, so its own single-entry `provisioningProfiles`
# overwrites ours wholesale. And there is no archive-only mode to hook between.
#
# So we let tauri produce its (broken) .ipa and simply export the archive AGAIN with a complete
# ExportOptions, overwriting it. `-exportArchive` re-signs every bundle from scratch, so the
# archive — which tauri leaves ad-hoc signed anyway — is a perfectly good input, and the second
# export costs seconds. This keeps the fix inside one recipe instead of forking the whole
# release lane away from tauri.
#
# No-ops for an app with no embedded extensions (admin-companion today), so both lanes share it.
_reexport-embedded-extensions app_dir:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    gen="{{app_dir}}/src-tauri/gen/apple"
    archive="$(ls -td "$gen"/build/*.xcarchive 2>/dev/null | head -n1 || true)"
    if [ -z "$archive" ]; then
      echo "✗ no .xcarchive under $gen/build — did the build actually run?" >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    app="$(ls -d "$archive"/Products/Applications/*.app 2>/dev/null | head -n1 || true)"
    if [ -z "$app" ]; then
      echo "✗ no .app inside $archive" >&2
      exit 1
    fi

    # Enumerate embedded bundles that need their own profile. Read from the archive rather than
    # assuming a name, so this keeps working if a second extension is ever added.
    appexes=()
    while IFS= read -r a; do [ -n "$a" ] && appexes+=("$a"); done < <(ls -d "$app"/PlugIns/*.appex 2>/dev/null || true)
    if [ "${#appexes[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
      echo "✓ no embedded extensions in $(basename "$app") — tauri's own export is complete"
      exit 0
    fi

    if [ -z "${IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE:-}" ]; then
      echo "✗ IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE is not set, but $(basename "$app") embeds an extension." >&2
      echo "  An app extension is a separate bundle and needs its OWN App Store provisioning" >&2
      echo "  profile, bound to its own App ID. Without it the extension ships with empty" >&2
      echo "  entitlements and App Store Connect rejects the upload." >&2
      echo "  Set it to the base64 of that .mobileprovision:" >&2
      echo "    export IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE=\"\$(base64 -i <profile>.mobileprovision)\"" >&2
      echo "  See docs/ios-cicd.md → \"Push notifications: three artifacts\"." >&2
      exit 1
    fi

    # Install the extension's profile where Xcode looks — the same folder and the same UUID
    # lookup tauri_macos_sign uses for the app's, so both are discoverable identically.
    profiles_dir="$HOME/Library/MobileDevice/Provisioning Profiles"
    mkdir -p "$profiles_dir"
    nse_profile="$(mktemp)"
    echo "$IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE" | base64 --decode > "$nse_profile"
    nse_plist="$(security cms -D -i "$nse_profile" 2>/dev/null)" || {
      echo "✗ IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE is not a decodable .mobileprovision" >&2; exit 1; }
    nse_uuid="$(plutil -extract UUID raw - <<<"$nse_plist")"
    team="$(plutil -extract TeamIdentifier.0 raw - <<<"$nse_plist")"

    # different profile than the archive was built against.

    app_uuid="$(grep -oE 'PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER = "[^"]+"' "$pbxproj" | head -n1 | sed -E 's/.*"(.*)"/\1/' || true)"

    export EXPORT_TEAM="$team" EXPORT_APP_ID="$app_id" EXPORT_APP_UUID="$app_uuid" EXPORT_NSE_UUID="$nse_uuid"
    options="$(mktemp -t ExportOptions).plist"
    profiles_json="$(for a in "${appexes[@]}"; do
      plutil -extract CFBundleIdentifier raw - <<<"$(plutil -convert xml1 -o - "$a/Info.plist")"
    done | paste -sd, -)"

    import os, plistlib, sys

    profiles = {os.environ["EXPORT_APP_ID"]: os.environ["EXPORT_APP_UUID"]}
    for bundle_id in filter(None, os.environ["EXPORT_APPEX_IDS"].split(",")):
        # Every extension shares one profile today (there is exactly one). A second extension
        # would need its own entry here and its own secret — the loop is where that lands.
        profiles[bundle_id] = os.environ["EXPORT_NSE_UUID"]

    options = {
        "method": "app-store-connect",
        "signingStyle": "manual",
        "teamID": os.environ["EXPORT_TEAM"],
        # The generic identity name, resolved by Xcode against the keychain — the same shape
        # tauri writes, and stable across cert renewals.
        "signingCertificate": "Apple Distribution",
        "provisioningProfiles": profiles,
    }
    with open(sys.argv[1], "wb") as handle:
        plistlib.dump(options, handle)
    print("  ExportOptions provisioningProfiles:")
    for bundle_id, uuid in profiles.items():
        print(f"    {bundle_id} -> {uuid}")
    PY

    echo "re-exporting $(basename "$archive") with profiles for every embedded bundle..."
    rm -f "$gen"/build/arm64/*.ipa
    xcodebuild -exportArchive \
      -archivePath "$archive" \
      -exportPath "$gen/build/arm64" \
      -exportOptionsPlist "$options" \
      -allowProvisioningUpdates >/dev/null
    rm -f "$options"
    echo "✓ re-exported with ${#appexes[@]} embedded extension(s) signed"

# Assert the exported .ipa is actually shippable: every bundle in it — the app and each
# embedded extension — must carry non-empty entitlements and its own embedded.mobileprovision.
#
# This is the check whose absence cost a full build-and-upload round trip. The failure it
# catches is completely silent locally: the archive succeeds, the export succeeds, the .ipa
# looks normal, and only App Store Connect objects, minutes later, with a 409. Two seconds of
# `codesign -d` turns that into an immediate local failure.
_verify-signed-ipa app_dir:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    ipa="$(ls -t "{{app_dir}}"/src-tauri/gen/apple/build/arm64/*.ipa 2>/dev/null | head -n1 || true)"
    if [ -z "$ipa" ]; then
      echo "✗ no .ipa to verify under {{app_dir}}/src-tauri/gen/apple/build/arm64/" >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    work="$(mktemp -d)"
    trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
    unzip -q "$ipa" -d "$work"
    app="$(ls -d "$work"/Payload/*.app | head -n1)"

    fail=0
    check() { # <bundle> <label>
      local bundle="$1" label="$2" ents
      if [ ! -f "$bundle/embedded.mobileprovision" ]; then
        echo "✗ $label has no embedded.mobileprovision — it was signed without a provisioning profile" >&2
        fail=1
      fi
      # `codesign -d --entitlements -` prints nothing (or an empty dict) when the bundle was
      # signed with none, which is exactly the state App Store Connect rejects.
      ents="$(codesign -d --entitlements - --xml "$bundle" 2>/dev/null || true)"
      if ! python3 -c '
    import plistlib, sys
    raw = sys.stdin.buffer.read()
    start = raw.find(b"<?xml")
    sys.exit(0 if start >= 0 and plistlib.loads(raw[start:]) else 1)
    ' <<<"$ents"; then
        echo "✗ $label has no code-signing entitlements (App Store Connect rejects this with a 409)" >&2
        fail=1
      else
        echo "  ✓ $label — entitlements present, profile embedded"
      fi
    }

    check "$app" "$(basename "$app")"
    for appex in "$app"/PlugIns/*.appex; do
      [ -d "$appex" ] || continue
      check "$appex" "PlugIns/$(basename "$appex")"
    done

    [ "$fail" -eq 0 ] || { echo "✗ $(basename "$ipa") is not shippable — see above" >&2; exit 1; }
    echo "✓ $(basename "$ipa") signing verified"

3. **GitHub secret** — base64 of that profile, wired into the wallet lane alongside

   be installed on the runner before `just ios-ipa` runs."""

new = """**Setting it up** (one time, mirroring the Admin Companion list above):

1. **App ID** — register `dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService`. No capabilities to
   enable: the extension's only entitlement is `keychain-access-groups`, which a profile
   authorizes through its `<TeamID>.*` wildcard. There is **no** App Store Connect app record —
   an extension ships inside its host app, not beside it.
2. **App Store provisioning profile** — a Distribution profile bound to that App ID, signed by
   the same Apple Distribution cert the wallet already uses.
3. **GitHub secret `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE`** — base64 of that profile
   (`base64 -i *.mobileprovision | pbcopy`). Unlike `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_ADMIN`, this is not an
   *alternative* to `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION` — both are used in the **same** build, because the app
   and the extension are separate bundles that each need their own profile.

### Why the release lane re-exports the archive

`cargo tauri ios build` archives and exports in one step, and its generated ExportOptions carries
exactly one provisioning-profile entry — the app's bundle id. It also only stamps signing
settings onto build-configuration lists whose comment contains `_iOS`, so an extension target is
left unsigned in the archive. `xcodebuild -exportArchive` then re-signs the extension with the
distribution identity but, having no profile for its bundle id, gives it **empty entitlements and
no embedded profile**.

Nothing fails along the way. The archive succeeds, the export succeeds, a normal-looking `.ipa`
lands on disk, and the first thing to object is App Store Connect, minutes later:

```
Validation failed (409) Missing Code Signing Entitlements. No entitlements found in bundle
'dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService' for executable '…/identity-wallet_NSE.appex/…'
```

The obvious escape hatch is closed: tauri merges a user-supplied `gen/apple/ExportOptions.plist`,
but its `merge_plist` is a shallow later-wins merge, so tauri's own single-entry
`provisioningProfiles` overwrites yours. There is also no archive-only mode to hook between.

So `just ios-ipa` runs `just _reexport-embedded-extensions` after the tauri build: it installs
the extension profile, reads the app's profile UUID out of the pbxproj tauri just stamped (so the
export uses exactly the profile the archive was built against), writes an ExportOptions naming a
profile for **every** embedded bundle, and re-exports over the `.ipa`. `-exportArchive` re-signs
everything from scratch, so the ad-hoc-signed archive is a fine input and the second export costs
seconds. It no-ops for an app with no extensions, so admin-companion shares the recipe untouched.

`just _verify-signed-ipa` then asserts every bundle in the `.ipa` — app and each `.appex` — has
non-empty entitlements and its own `embedded.mobileprovision`. That check exists because this
failure is invisible locally; without it the only signal is a 409 after a full upload."""
