Done and pushed.

## What the artifacts showed

Your rejected IPA was still on disk, so I diagnosed from it rather than theory:

- Archive's `.appex`: **"code object is not signed at all"**
- Exported `.appex`: signed with your identity, but **`<dict></dict>`** entitlements and no `embedded.mobileprovision`
- The app beside it: perfect — `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)` expanded, `aps-environment` → `production`, keychain groups correctly ordered

Both halves are tauri-cli: it stamps signing only onto `_iOS`-named targets, and writes one `provisioningProfiles` entry. The `gen/apple/ExportOptions.plist` escape hatch is closed — `merge_plist` is shallow later-wins, so tauri's single entry overwrites yours.

## The fix

`just ios-ipa` now re-exports the archive with an ExportOptions naming a profile for **every** embedded bundle, reading the app's profile UUID from the pbxproj tauri just stamped so the export matches what was archived. It no-ops for apps without extensions, so admin-companion is untouched.

`just _verify-signed-ipa` then asserts every bundle has entitlements and a profile — run against your rejected IPA it reproduces both defects and fails. That's the check that would have caught this locally instead of at Apple.

CI wiring: `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE`, optional on the reusable workflow, passed only by the wallet caller. So last turn's answer now has a real resolution — the name is correct *because this commit writes the consumer*.

## What I verified vs. didn't

Locally exercised: the missing-profile guard, the no-extension no-op, and the full pipeline — decode, UUID/team extraction, install, ExportOptions generation, `xcodebuild -exportArchive`. Fed your app profile as a stand-in it failed on exactly `has app ID dev.malpercio.identitywallet, which does not match the bundle ID …NotificationService` — Xcode confirming it now consults a per-bundle profile.

**Not verified: a successful signed export.** No profile for that bundle id exists on this machine, so that's yours:

1. App ID `dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService` — no capabilities
2. Distribution profile bound to it, same cert
3. `export IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE="$(base64 -i <profile>.mobileprovision)"` then `just ios-release`

If it works, `_verify-signed-ipa` prints a ✓ per bundle before altool runs.

One caveat worth stating: I predicted this would fail at archive/export, and it didn't — it produced a plausible IPA that only Apple rejected. So "the build succeeded" has proven a poor signal here twice now, which is why the verification step matters more than the fix.

Confirmed — `signing_from_env()` returns `(None, None)` when `IOS_CERTIFICATE`/`IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`/`IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION` are unset, which drops tauri into automatic signing and the placeholder cert. **This is an environment problem, not a defect** — and it's my fault: I told you to export only `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE`, omitting the three you'd had set in the 20:50 run.

Let me make that failure impossible to hit silently.

input.old_string:
bv="{{build_number}}"
    [ -n "$bv" ] || bv="$(date -u +%s)"
input.new_string:
# Pre-flight the signing environment BEFORE the ~10-minute build.
    #
    # tauri's `signing_from_env()` reads exactly these three and silently returns "no signing"
    # if any is missing — it does not error. The build then runs to completion under AUTOMATIC
    # signing, mints the placeholder cert `Apple Distribution: Tauri (unset)` (tauri#11092), and
    # dies at the very end with `No signing certificate "iOS Distribution" found`, which names
    # neither the real cause nor the variable to set. One forgotten `export` in a fresh shell
    # therefore costs a full build and produces a misleading error; this costs a second.
    missing=()
    [ -n "${IOS_CERTIFICATE:-}" ] || missing+=("IOS_CERTIFICATE")
    # Set-but-empty is legitimate for a .p12 exported without a password, so test for the
    # variable's existence rather than its content.
    [ -n "${IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD+x}" ] || missing+=("IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD")
    [ -n "${IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION:-}" ] || missing+=("IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION")
    if [ "${#missing[@]}" -gt 0 ]; then
      echo "✗ signing is not configured — missing: ${missing[*]}" >&2
      echo "  This lane signs EXPLICITLY; tauri's automatic signing produces an" >&2
      echo "  \"Apple Distribution: Tauri (unset)\" placeholder that App Store Connect rejects." >&2
      echo "  With these unset the build would run to completion and only then fail." >&2
      echo >&2
      echo "  export IOS_CERTIFICATE=\"\$(base64 -i Distribution.p12)\"" >&2
      echo "  export IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD='…'" >&2
      echo "  export IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION=\"\$(base64 -i <app>.mobileprovision)\"" >&2
      echo "  export IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE=\"\$(base64 -i <extension>.mobileprovision)\"  # apps embedding an extension" >&2
      echo >&2
      echo "  See docs/ios-cicd.md → \"GitHub repo secrets\"." >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    bv="{{build_number}}"
    [ -n "$bv" ] || bv="$(date -u +%s)"

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && git add -A && git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit -F - <<'MSG'
Pre-flight the iOS signing environment before the build

A local release run failed at the very end with:

    found cert "Apple Distribution: Tauri (unset)" with organization "Tauri"
    error: exportArchive No signing certificate "iOS Distribution" found

That is tauri's automatic-signing placeholder (tauri#11092) — the exact thing this
lane signs explicitly to avoid. The cause was simply that IOS_CERTIFICATE,
IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD and IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION were not set in that shell.

The failure mode is what makes it worth guarding. `signing_from_env()` does not error
on absent variables; it returns "no signing", the build runs to completion under
automatic signing, and the export dies with a message that names neither the real cause
nor the variable to set. One forgotten export in a fresh terminal therefore costs a
full build and hands back a misleading error. The same three variables are what the
already-added extension re-export reads a profile UUID from, so this also stops that
step reporting a confusing secondary failure.

`just ios-ipa` now checks all three up front and refuses in about a second, printing
the exports to run. IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD is tested for existence rather than
content, since a .p12 exported without a password is legitimate.

The troubleshooting entry for the placeholder cert now carries the full local
environment, including the extension profile — the previous text named the three
variables but never showed a working shell setup, which is the form the mistake takes.
